summary: Describes how to store E.164 telephone numbers in the Domain Name System so a phone number can be mapped to Internet services. It was later replaced by RFC 3761.

eli5.summary: Phone numbers can be turned into a special Internet name so a computer can look up how to reach that person online.

questions: how to look up phone numbers in dns
how do phone numbers work in dns
subtitle: Turn a telephone number into a DNS name, then look up the Internet services that reach that number.

tldr.problem: A telephone number says nothing about which Internet services (SIP, email, web) can reach its owner, and there was no decentralized way to look that up.
tldr.mechanism: The E.164 number is turned into a name under e164.arpa by reversing its digits, and the DNS NAPTR records stored there rewrite the number into one or more URIs.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2916 was a Proposed Standard but has been replaced by RFC 3761, which is the version to read today.

today: RFC 2916 was a Proposed Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 3761, which is the current specification to read.

sections.title: Why Put Phone Numbers in DNS
sections.content:
RFC 2916 describes how the Domain Name System (DNS) can store E.164 telephone numbers, so that a client can find which services are available for one number. It uses delegation through NS records and NAPTR records, which lets the lookup be decentralized, with each level managed by a different party.

The scope is narrow. The RFC covers finding the services only. Routing of the actual connection using the selected service is not discussed.
sections.eli5: It is like a phone book that does not just list a phone number but also lists the other ways to reach that person. Different people look after different pages of the book.

sections.title: From Phone Number to DNS Name
sections.content:
The domain e164.arpa holds the numbers and is divided into subdomains to allow distributed operation. The client builds the name in six steps:

  1. Write the number in full form with the country code, for example +46-8-9761234.
  2. Remove all non-digit characters except the leading +, giving +4689761234.
  3. Remove everything except the digits: 4689761234.
  4. Put a dot between each digit: 4.6.8.9.7.6.1.2.3.4.
  5. Reverse the order of the digits: 4.3.2.1.6.7.9.8.6.4.
  6. Append .e164.arpa: 4.3.2.1.6.7.9.8.6.4.e164.arpa.

The + is kept after step 2 to flag that the string is an E.164 number. The RFC says other numbering plans, such as closed ones, may need a similar mechanism, but that is future work. Number holders who want to be listed contact the zone administrator found in the zone's SOA record, and listing policies may differ in different parts of the world.
sections.eli5: You write the phone number's digits backwards with dots between them, then add .e164.arpa at the end. That gives a name a computer can look up.

sections.title: NAPTR Records and the E2U Service
sections.content:
The name is looked up with NAPTR records. Their key fields are order (records MUST be processed in this order), preference (the order SHOULD be followed among records with the same order), service, flags, regexp and replacement. The URIs are stored in the regexp field.

The input to the algorithm is the E.164 number from step 2, with only the leading + and digits. The output is an absolute URI. The service used is called E2U (E.164 to URI), which maps one E.164 number to a list of URIs. Its listed error conditions are a number not in the numbering plan, a number with no URIs, and an unavailable service.

The client applies all the substitutions and performs all the lookups. They are not done by the DNS servers.
sections.eli5: The lookup gives back a short list of ways to reach the person. Each item says what kind of way it is, and your own computer follows the instructions on the list.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
In the first example, the name 4.3.2.1.6.7.9.8.6.4.e164.arpa has two records. One gives sip:info@tele2.se and the other mailto:info@tele2.se. The lower order value on the SIP record means the number is preferably contacted by SIP, and secondly by SMTP. The client then uses each protocol's own resolution to find the node to contact.

A record may also return a tel URI. In that case the procedure is restarted with the new E.164 number, and the client is responsible for loop detection.

A third example places a wildcard at 6.4.e164.arpa. It says that information about all numbers in the 46 country code is in an LDAP server, and the regular expression picks the search to run.

Appendix A walks through a full scenario. The regulator delegates 6.4 to a name server, hands a block of 10000 numbers to a telco, and the telco in turn points to a company named Redirection Service for one subscriber's number. That service holds SIP, mailto, http and tel records. The calling client knows SIP, so it picks the SIP record and applies the regular expression to +4689761234 to get sip:sven@sips.se.
sections.eli5: Say you look up a number and get back a list: first try the Internet phone address, then try email. You try them in that order, like asking for someone at their desk first and leaving a note second.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC asks IANA to delegate the e164.arpa domain following instructions from the IAB. Names are to be hierarchic and assigned in line with ITU Recommendation E.164. Delegations directly in the zone are done after Expert Review, with a designated expert appointed by the IESG.

Because the system sits on DNS, the answers are no more trustworthy than any DNS answer, so the RFC recommends DNSSEC. Two dangers are named for the E2U service: malicious redirection (a bad entry sends clients to the wrong URI) and denial of service (removing the URI so the resource cannot be reached).

Caching means a change takes as long to propagate as the time to live of the NAPTR records. The RFC warns this needs great care where IP addresses are for hire, such as with DHCP. Where several providers compete for routing and translation, changes need identification, authentication and authorization.
sections.eli5: If someone sneaks a fake entry into the book, people could be sent to the wrong place. So the entries need to be signed and only the right people should be allowed to change them.
